title: Functions, recursion & first array assignments
overview: This module introduces functions, which package logic into small reusable pieces, and recursion, a function that calls itself with a smaller problem. Where the recursive call sits decides the output order. It ends with the first array assignments (in C++ with `vector`): duplicates, prefix sums, a sorted check, inserting one array into another, and printing an X pattern.

concepts.explain: A named block with inputs (parameters) and an output (return value). `int sum(int x, int y) { return x + y; }`

concepts.term: Pass by value vs by pointer
concepts.explain: C copies arguments into the function. To change the caller's variables, pass their addresses (`&x`) and write through the pointers (`*x = ...`).
Every recursive function needs a stopping condition, for example `if (x > n) return;`. Without one, it calls itself until the stack overflows.

concepts.term: Print before vs after the call
concepts.explain: Printing before the recursive call gives the order 1..N. Printing after the call prints while the calls return, which gives N..1.
`sum(i) = a[i] + sum(i+1)`, and the sum past the end is 0.
After sorting, equal values sit next to each other, so a duplicate check only needs to compare `A[i]` with `A[i-1]`.
`pre[i] = pre[i-1] + a[i]` stores the running total up to index `i`. Use `long long`, because the totals grow quickly.
`A.insert(A.begin() + X, value)` shifts later elements right and puts `value` at index X.

files.title: Add (with a function)
files.what: Reads two numbers and prints their sum, using a helper function `sum`.
steps: `sum(int x, int y)` returns `x + y`.
`main` reads `x` and `y`, calls `sum(x, y)`, and stores the result in `result`.
Print `result`.
files.output_note: It prints the prompt `Enter two numbers: ` and then `7`.
files.watch_out: The prompt `Enter two numbers: ` is extra output, so an online judge would mark this Wrong Answer. Remove prompts before submitting.

files.title: Swap (with pointers)
files.what: Swaps two numbers inside a function by passing their addresses.
steps: `swap(int *x, int *y)` receives the addresses of the caller's variables.
`temp = *x` saves the first value.
`*x = *y` copies the second value into the first variable, then `*y = temp` finishes the swap.
`main` calls `swap(&x, &y)` and prints `x y`.
files.output_note: Input `5 2` prints `2 5`: the variables in `main` really were swapped.

check.q: Why wouldn't `void swap(int x, int y)` work?
check.a: It would swap copies. The variables in `main` would not change.

files.title: Recursion: 1 to N
files.what: Prints 1 to N by printing the current number and then calling itself with `x+1`.
steps: The base case is `x > n`: return.
Otherwise print `x`, then call `print_1_to_N(x+1, n)`.
Because the print comes before the call, the numbers come out in increasing order.
files.complexity: Time O(n) · Space O(n) call stack
files.output_note: After the prompt you see `1 2 3 4 5 ` (with a trailing space).

check.q: What is the base case here?

files.title: Recursion: N to 1
files.what: The same recursion, but the print comes after the recursive call, so the numbers come out in reverse as the calls return.
steps: The base case is `x > n`: return.
Call `print_N_to_1(x+1, n)` first.
Print `x` only after that call returns. The deepest call (x = n) prints first.
files.complexity: Time O(n) · Space O(n) call stack

check.q: What single change turns the 1-to-N program into this one?
check.a: Move the `printf` after the recursive call.

files.title: Print Recursion (N times)
files.what: Prints `I love Recursion` N times by counting `n` down to 0 through recursive calls.
steps: If `n == 0`, return.
Print the line once.
Call `printRecursion(n-1)`.
files.output_note: The line appears 3 times, once for each call with n = 3, 2, 1.

check.q: How many calls happen in total for n = 3, including the base case?

files.title: Print from 1 to N (judge version)
files.what: The judge version of the 1-to-N recursion. It has no prompt and prints each number on its own line.
steps: The recursion is the same as in recursion_print_1_to_N.c.
It uses `%d\n` so each number is on a separate line, as the task asks.
files.output_note: It prints 1 to 5, one number per line, exactly as the judge expects.

check.q: Why is the prompt removed in this version?
check.a: The judge compares output exactly, so any extra text is wrong.

files.title: Print from N to 1 (no trailing space)
files.what: The judge version of N-to-1. It prints `1` last without a space after it, so the line has no trailing space.
steps: Recurse first, then print.
If `x > 1`, print `x` followed by a space. If `x == 1`, which is the last number printed, print it with no space.
files.output_note: It prints `4 3 2 1`, with no space after the 1.

check.q: Which number is printed last, and why does that matter here?
check.a: `1`, because it is the outermost call. It is the one printed without a trailing space.

files.title: Sum of an array with recursion
files.what: Adds up an array recursively: the sum from index `i` is `a[i]` plus the sum from `i+1`.
steps: The array `a` is global, so the function can read it.
`getSum(i, n)` returns 0 when `i == n` (past the end).
Otherwise it returns `a[i] + getSum(i+1, n)`.
`main` calls `getSum(0, n)`.
files.complexity: Time O(n) · Space O(n) call stack

check.q: What does `getSum(4, 5)` return for this input?

files.title: Assignment: any duplicate?
files.what: Sorts the array, then checks neighbouring pairs. If any two neighbours are equal, the array has a duplicate.
steps: Read `n` numbers into `vector<int> A`.
`sort(A.begin(), A.end())` places equal values next to each other.
For `i` from 1, if `A[i] == A[i-1]`, print `YES` and stop.
If the loop finishes without a match, print `NO`.
files.complexity: Time O(n log n) · Space O(n)
files.output_note: After sorting, the array is `1 1 2 2 3 5`. The first pair `1 1` matches, so it prints `YES`.

check.q: Why is sorting needed before the neighbour check?
check.a: Without sorting, equal values can be far apart, so comparing neighbours would miss them.

files.title: Assignment: prefix sums in reverse
files.what: Builds the running-sum (prefix sum) array and prints it from the last element to the first.
steps: Read the values into `vector<long long> nums`.
`runningSum[0] = nums[0]`, then `runningSum[i] = runningSum[i-1] + nums[i]`.
Loop `i` from `n-1` down to 0 and print each value.
files.input_note: n, then the array (the task's sample).
files.output_note: The prefix sums are 2 6 7 12 15. Printed in reverse, they give `15 12 7 6 2`.

check.a: The values go up to 10^9 and n up to 10^5, so the sums can reach 10^14, far beyond `int`.

files.title: Prefix sums in reverse (re-typed)
files.what: A practice re-typing of the prefix-sum assignment. The logic is identical.
steps: The steps are the same as in assignment_2_get_prefix_sum.cpp.
files.output_note: This input shows why `long long` is needed: the output is `3000000000 2000000000 1000000000`.

check.q: What would go wrong if `runningSum` were `vector<int>`?
check.a: 3×10^9 would overflow and print as a negative number.

files.title: Assignment: is the array sorted?
files.what: For each test case, checks whether every element is at least as large as the one before it.
steps: Read `T`, then for each test read `N` and the array.
Start with `flag = true`.
If any `A[j] < A[j-1]`, set `flag = false` and `break`.
Print `YES` if `flag` is still true, otherwise `NO`.
files.complexity: Time O(N) per test · Space O(N)
files.input_note: T test cases, each with N and then N values.
files.output_note: The output is `YES`, `YES` (equal neighbours still count as sorted), then `NO` (because 1 < 100).

check.q: Is `1 1 2 2` sorted by this program's rule? Why?
check.a: Yes. The program only rejects the array when an element is strictly smaller than the one before it.

files.title: Sorted check (re-typed)
files.what: A practice re-typing of the sorted-array assignment with the same logic.
steps: The steps are the same as in assignment_3_sorted.cpp.
files.complexity: Time O(N) per test · Space O(N)
files.output_note: `YES` for the increasing array, `NO` for the decreasing one.

check.a: Once one out-of-order pair is found, checking the rest is pointless.

files.title: Assignment: insert array B into A at X
files.what: Inserts every element of `B` into `A`, starting at index `X`, and keeps B's order by moving `X` forward after each insert.
steps: Read `A` (size N), `B` (size M) and `X`.
For each `B[i]`, `A.insert(A.begin() + X, B[i])`, then `X++`, so the next element goes right after it.
Print all `N+M` elements.
files.input_note: N, A, M, B, X (the task's sample).
files.output_note: 10, 20 and 30 end up starting at index 3: `2 3 4 10 20 30 5 6`.

check.q: What would happen if you forgot `X++`?
check.a: Each new element would go in front of the previous one, so B would appear reversed: `30 20 10`.

files.title: Insert array (re-typed)
files.what: A practice re-typing of Insert it. Only the names N and M are swapped.
steps: The steps are the same as in assignment_4_insert_it.cpp.
files.output_note: With `X = 0`, B goes at the front: `10 20 30 3 4 5 6`.

check.q: How could you insert all of B in one call?

files.title: Assignment: print an X pattern
files.what: Prints an X of height N (N is odd) using spaces, `\` and `/`, counting the spaces on each row.
steps: If `N == 1`, just print `X`.
Upper half (N/2 rows): row `i` prints `i` spaces, then `\`, then `spaces` gap, then `/`. The gap starts at `N-2` and shrinks by 2 each row.
Middle row: `N/2` spaces, then `X`.
Lower half: the outer spaces shrink by 1 and the middle gap grows by 2, with `/` before `\`.
files.output_note: Seven rows form an X, and the `X` sits in the middle row (row 4).
files.watch_out: In C++, a backslash has to be written as `"\\"` in a string. A single `\` starts an escape sequence.

check.q: For N = 7, how many spaces are between `\` and `/` in the first row?

files.title: X pattern (re-typed)
files.what: A practice re-typing of Printing X with the same logic (it even has a harmless extra `;`).
steps: The steps are the same as in assignment_5_printing_X.cpp.
files.output_note: For N = 5 there are two rows above the `X` and two below it.

check.q: Where is the `X` placed for N = 5?

recap: Functions take copies of their arguments; pass pointers to change the caller's variables.
Every recursive function needs a base case.
Print before the recursive call for 1 to N, and after it for N to 1.
Sort, then compare neighbours, to find duplicates.
Prefix sum: `pre[i] = pre[i-1] + a[i]`, stored in `long long`.
Remove prompts and trailing spaces before submitting to a judge.

check_yourself.q: What happens if a recursive function has no base case?
check_yourself.a: It keeps calling itself until the call stack runs out, and the program crashes with a stack overflow.

check_yourself.q: How do you print N to 1 with recursion while counting x upward from 1?
check_yourself.a: Make the recursive call first and print `x` after it returns.

check_yourself.q: Write a recursive formula for the sum of the first n numbers.

check_yourself.a: It passes the addresses of `x` and `y`, so the function can change the originals.
